C003.subject: GDP per capita
C003.object: subjective wellbeing, social cohesion, and environmental health
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita subjective wellbeing, social cohesion, and environmental health]

[CONFLICT] The claim that GDP per capita fails to capture subjective wellbeing, social cohesion, and environmental health is disputed because GDP is a narrow economic measure that omits non-market factors and inequality, which are critical for holistic welfare assessment in post-industrial societies.

C004.object: a more comprehensive proxy for human wellbeing than GDP per capita
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Alternative indices (e.g., HDI, GPI) a more comprehensive proxy for human wellbeing than GDP per capita]

qualifier.tension: creates epistemic friction by challenging the primacy of GDP

C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: material living standards in developed economies after 2000
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in developed economies after 2000]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and national accounts data (e.g., real household disposable income per capita vs. GDP per capita) — Directly compares GDP per capita growth with alternative measures of material living standards (e.g., median income, consumption, housing quality) for developed economies post-2000 to quantify divergence.

[PATH:literature] Studies on inequality-adjusted human development index (IHDI) and inclusive wealth index for OECD countries — Reviews existing empirical research that tests whether GDP per capita overstates improvements in material well-being due to rising inequality, depreciation of natural capital, or changes in household composition.

[PATH:empirical] Micro-level panel data from surveys like the Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) or EU-SILC tracking household consumption and wealth — Provides micro-level evidence on whether aggregate GDP growth translates into improved material conditions for typical households, directly testing the divergence hypothesis at the individual level.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
C006.object: material living standards in developed economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in developed economies]

[PATH:empirical] Maddison Project Database (historical GDP per capita and real income data for developed economies, 1900-1999) — Provides longitudinal GDP per capita data that can be directly compared with alternative welfare indicators (e.g., life expectancy, education, leisure time) to test correlation with material living standards.

[PATH:empirical] Human Development Index (HDI) time series for OECD countries (1900-1999) — Offers a composite measure of material living standards beyond GDP; comparing HDI trends with GDP per capita over the century can reveal decoupling or correlation patterns.

[PATH:literature] Literature review on the Easterlin Paradox and beyond: e.g., Easterlin (1974) and subsequent critiques (e.g., Stevenson & Wolfers, 2008) — Directly addresses the disputed relationship between income growth and subjective well-being or living standards in developed economies, providing theoretical and empirical context for the hypothesis.

C007.subject: GDP per capita
C007.object: social cohesion in post-industrial societies when inequality exceeds a threshold of 0.4 Gini
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita social cohesion in post-industrial societies when inequality exceeds a threshold of 0.4 Gini]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Income Distribution Database (IDD) merged with World Values Survey (WVS) data on social trust and civic engagement for post-2000 OECD countries — Provides cross-national, time-series data on Gini coefficients and social cohesion indicators (e.g., generalized trust, group membership) to test the threshold effect at Gini > 0.4.

[PATH:literature] Wilkinson & Pickett (2009) 'The Spirit Level' and subsequent replication studies using updated post-2000 data — Key theoretical and empirical foundation for the inequality-cohesion link; reviewing later critiques and re-analyses can clarify whether the GDP per capita inverse correlation holds specifically above a 0.4 Gini threshold in post-industrial societies.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of regional GDP per capita and social cohesion indices (e.g., Social Cohesion Radar) for OECD countries, controlling for welfare state regimes — Allows testing of the conditional hypothesis by comparing regions with Gini above and below 0.4, while accounting for institutional factors that may moderate the relationship.

C008.subject: GDP per capita
C008.object: improvements in subjective wellbeing, social cohesion, and environmental health
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita improvements in subjective wellbeing, social cohesion, and environmental health]

[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey (WVS) and European Social Survey (ESS) longitudinal data on subjective wellbeing and social trust, merged with World Bank GDP per capita data for 1990–2020 — Allows direct cross-national and temporal correlation analysis between GDP per capita and individual-level measures of happiness, life satisfaction, and social cohesion, controlling for confounds like inequality and institutional quality.

[PATH:empirical] Environmental Performance Index (EPI) and Ecological Footprint data combined with GDP per capita trends in post-industrial societies — Tests the environmental health component by examining whether GDP growth correlates with improvements in air/water quality, biodiversity, and resource efficiency, or whether decoupling is observed only in certain policy contexts.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of the Easterlin Paradox literature (e.g., Easterlin et al., 2010; Sacks, Stevenson & Wolfers, 2012) — Synthesizes conflicting evidence on whether GDP per capita gains produce lasting improvements in subjective wellbeing, especially beyond a threshold, and clarifies conditions under which social cohesion and environmental health co-vary with growth.

C009.subject: Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)
C009.object: long-term national life satisfaction trends than GDP per capita in post-industrial economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) long-term national life satisfaction trends than GDP per capita in post-industrial economies]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal GPI and life satisfaction datasets for OECD countries (e.g., from the Genuine Progress Indicator project at the University of Vermont or the OECD Better Life Index) — Directly comparing time-series correlations between GPI per capita and national life satisfaction (e.g., World Happiness Report) versus GDP per capita over 2000-2025 would test predictive strength in post-industrial economies.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on alternative welfare metrics and subjective well-being (e.g., Easterlin paradox literature, Kahneman & Krueger 2006, or recent reviews in Social Indicators Research) — Synthesizing existing empirical findings on GPI, GDP, and life satisfaction would reveal whether GPI consistently outperforms GDP in explaining long-term trends, especially in countries with high income but stagnant well-being.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework linking GPI components (e.g., income inequality, environmental costs, unpaid work) to mechanisms of life satisfaction (e.g., adaptation, social comparison, hedonic treadmill) — Developing or reviewing a causal model that explains why GPI should better capture non-material determinants of well-being would provide a priori justification for empirical tests and help interpret results.

C010.subject: GDP per capita
C010.object: the most reliable and universally applicable measure of economic success and indirectly, human wellbeing
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita the most reliable and universally applicable measure of economic success and indirectly, human wellbeing]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative analysis of GDP per capita vs. Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and Human Development Index (HDI) across 100+ countries over 2000-2023 — Directly tests whether GDP per capita correlates consistently with broader wellbeing measures; high divergence would refute its universal applicability.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of literature on alternative economic indicators (e.g., Genuine Progress Indicator, Gross National Happiness, Inclusive Wealth Index) and their cross-national predictive validity for health, education, and life satisfaction — Synthesizes existing evidence on whether GDP per capita outperforms or underperforms alternatives in predicting human wellbeing across diverse national contexts.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of GDP measurement biases in non-market economies, informal sectors, and subsistence agriculture (e.g., sub-Saharan Africa, rural Asia) — Evaluates structural limitations of GDP per capita as a universal metric; if systematic biases are severe, it cannot be universally reliable.
